slides.title: From IP to the Wire — The Missing Link
slides.body:
Why the Data Link Layer Exists?
IP knows where to send a packet. But how does a packet actually travel from one device to its immediate neighbor,  across a wire, a WiFi signal, or a cable?
That is exactly what the Data Link Layer solves

slides.title: The Data Link Layer
slides.body:
Analogy
Analogy:
The Data Link Layer is like the local courier service within a city. The Network Layer (IP) is the national logistics company that plans a package's journey from source to destination across cities. But the local courier handles each delivery within the city — picks up the package, checks local addresses (MAC), avoids traffic (access control), reports if a delivery failed (error detection). Different job, same package.

slides.title: Framing — Packaging Bits for the Physical Layer
slides.body:
Why Frames Exist?
The Physical Layer transmits raw bits — a continuous stream of 0s and 1s. It has no concept of where one message ends and another begins
Framing solves this problem. The Data Link Layer groups bits into meaningful units called frames. A frame has a defined start, a body (the payload), and a defined end — so the receiver knows exactly where each unit begins and ends

slides.title: 1. Character Count — Simplest Framing Method
slides.body:
Critical Problem — Error in Count Field:
If the count field itself is corrupted during transmission, the receiver reads the wrong count.
It then grabs the wrong number of bytes, completely losing track of where frames begin and end.
This is called framing error or loss of frame synchronization — and it cascades: all subsequent frames are misread.
This fatal weakness is why Character Count is rarely used in practice for reliable communication.

slides.title: 2. Byte Stuffing — Using Delimiters to Mark Frames
slides.body:
FLAG, ESC, and the Art of Escaping
The Problem this Solves:
If the data payload happens to contain the same bit pattern as the FLAG byte, the receiver would wrongly think the frame ended. Byte Stuffing prevents this

slides.title: 2. Byte Stuffing — Using Delimiters to Mark Frames
slides.body:
FLAG, ESC, and the Art of Escaping
How Byte Stuffing Works?
The sender scans the data payload before sending
If a FLAG byte appears in the data → insert an ESC byte before it
If an ESC byte appears in the data → insert another ESC byte before it
Receiver reverses the process: sees ESC → treats the next byte as data (not a delimiter), removes the ESC

slides.title: 2. Byte Stuffing — Using Delimiters to Mark Frames
slides.body:
Analogy
Analogy:
Byte Stuffing is like writing a legal document where certain words are reserved keywords — 'END', 'ESC'. If the document text needs to use the word 'END', the lawyer puts a special marker before it: [ESCAPE] END — telling the reader: 'this is not the end of the document, it is just the word end in the text.' The reader knows to look for the escape marker and treat the next word as regular content.

slides.title: 3. Bit Stuffing
slides.body:
Introduction
Bit Stuffing is used in bit-oriented protocols (like HDLC, High-Level Data Link Control). Instead of working with bytes, it works at the individual bit level
Flag Pattern: 01111110 (six consecutive 1s surrounded by 0s)
This specific pattern marks the start and end of a frame

slides.title: 3. Bit Stuffing
slides.body:
Introduction
Problem
If the data payload contains the bit pattern 01111110 or even just six consecutive 1s, the receiver would wrongly detect a frame boundary

slides.title: 3. Bit Stuffing
slides.body:
Introduction
How Bit Stuffing Works:
Sender Rule: After every five consecutive 1s in the data payload, the sender automatically inserts a 0
Receiver Rule: After every five consecutive 1s, if the next bit is 0, remove it (it was stuffed). If the next bit is 1 followed by 0 → it is the FLAG (frame end). If the next bit is 1 followed by 1 → it is an error (abort sequence)

Analogy
Analogy:
Bit Stuffing is like a rule in Morse code: if you ever accidentally tap five dots in a row, you must insert a deliberate pause (0) so the listener knows the next dots are still part of the message — not the special 'end of message' signal. The listener knows the rule and removes the pause when replaying the message.

slides.title: MAC Address — The Physical Address of a Device
slides.body:
48-bit Hardware Address
A MAC address (Media Access Control Address) is a unique hardware identifier assigned to every Network Interface Card (NIC). It is a physical address, burned into the hardware at the time of manufacture

slides.title: MAC Address — The Physical Address of a Device
slides.body:
48-bit Hardware Address
Key Properties of a MAC Address
Size: 48 bits (6 bytes)
Format: Written as six pairs of hexadecimal digits separated by colons or hyphens. Example: 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E
Uniqueness: Every NIC in the world is assigned a unique MAC address
Scope: MAC addresses are local, used only within the same network segment (LAN). They are not routed across networks
Layer: Data Link Layer

Analogy:
A MAC address is like the serial number of a car — stamped into the chassis at the factory, unique worldwide, and never changes. An IP address is like a license plate — assigned by the government (your ISP or network admin), tied to where the car is registered, and can change when the car moves to a different state. The serial number identifies the car itself; the license plate identifies where it is registered.

Key observation — In an ARP Request
The Target MAC Address field is 00:00:00:00:00:00 — all zeros. This is because the whole point of the request is that the sender does NOT know the target MAC yet

The Target MAC Address field is now filled in with the actual MAC. This is the answer being returned

slides.title: ARP at Every Hop
slides.body:
Source IP and Destination IP → never change end-to-end across the entire journey
Why MAC Addresses Keep Changing
Source MAC and Destination MAC → change at every single hop
This is one of the most important and most misunderstood concepts in networking

slides.title: ARP at Every Hop
slides.body:
Why MAC Addresses Keep Changing
MAC addresses are local. They are only meaningful on one network segment. As soon as a packet crosses a router, the router strips the old frame (and its MAC addresses), looks at the IP header, makes a routing decision, and builds a brand new frame with new MAC addresses for the next segment
ARP is what makes this possible at every hop

slides.title: ARP at Every Hop

Analogy
Analogy: Imagine a relay race. The packet (IP packet) carries the same runner numbers (source IP, destination IP) all through the race. But the person holding the packet (MAC address) changes at every exchange point (router). Before each handoff, the runners ask, "Are you the next runner? What’s your lane number?" (ARP). The packet’s label stays the same, but the person holding it keeps changing..
